days.title: Descent with Modification & Common Ancestry
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define descent with modification.
  • Explain common ancestry.
  • Describe how species diverge over time.
  • Relate phylogeny to evolutionary history.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Descent with modification — species change over time and share common ancestors.
  • Common ancestry — all life shares a common ancestor.
  • Phylogeny — evolutionary history of a species.
  • Speciation — formation of new species.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Descent with Modification

Darwin proposed that species change over time through natural selection, and that all species descend from common ancestors.

B. Common Ancestry

  • All life shares fundamental features (DNA, ribosomes, ATP)
  • Similarities reflect shared ancestry
  • Differences reflect adaptations

C. Phylogeny

Phylogenetic trees show evolutionary relationships. The base represents a common ancestor; branches represent lineages.

days.title: Development of Evolutionary Thought
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Trace the history of evolutionary thought.
  • Compare Lamarck's and Darwin's ideas.
  • Explain Darwin's contributions.
  • Describe the modern synthesis.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Lamarckism — inheritance of acquired characteristics (disproven).
  • Darwinism — natural selection as the mechanism of evolution.
  • Modern synthesis — combines Darwinism with genetics.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Early Thinkers

  • Linnaeus — classification system
  • Cuvier — fossils, catastrophism
  • Lamarck — inheritance of acquired characteristics
  • Malthus — populations grow faster than resources

B. Darwin & Wallace

  • Voyage of the HMS Beagle (1831–1836)
  • Observations in the Galápagos Islands
  • On the Origin of Species (1859)
  • Natural selection as the mechanism

C. Modern Synthesis

  • Combines Darwin's natural selection with Mendel's genetics
  • Explains how variation arises
  • Forms the basis of modern biology

days.title: Evidence of Evolution
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe multiple lines of evidence for evolution.
  • Explain biogeography.
  • Describe the fossil record.
  • Explain homology and molecular evidence.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Biogeography — geographic distribution of species.
  • Fossil record — preserved remains showing past life.
  • Homology — similar structures from common ancestry.
  • Molecular evidence — DNA/protein similarities.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Lines of Evidence

TypeExample
BiogeographyIsland species resemble mainland species
Fossil recordTransitional fossils (e.g., Archaeopteryx)
Comparative anatomyHomologous structures (forelimbs of mammals)
Comparative embryologyEmbryos of related species look similar
Molecular biologyDNA/protein sequence similarities
Direct observationAntibiotic resistance in bacteria

B. Vestigial Structures

  • Structures with reduced function
  • Examples: human appendix, whale pelvic bones

scenarios.text: Forelimbs of humans, whales, and bats share a similar bone pattern.
Island species resemble nearby mainland species.

takeaways: Six lines of evidence support evolution.

days.title: Inferring Evolutionary Relationships
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Use evidence to infer relationships.
  • Explain how molecular data builds trees.
  • Describe how fossils fill gaps.
  • Interpret phylogenetic trees.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Phylogenetic tree — diagram of evolutionary relationships.
  • Node — common ancestor point.
  • Clade — ancestor + all descendants.
  • Molecular clock — uses DNA differences to estimate time.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Inferring Relationships

  • Compare anatomy, embryology, DNA, fossils
  • Shared features → shared ancestry
  • More shared features → closer relationship

B. Molecular Clocks

Assume mutation rate is roughly constant over time. The more differences in DNA, the longer ago two species diverged.

C. Reading a Phylogenetic Tree

  • Nodes = common ancestors
  • Branch length = time or amount of change
  • Tips = present-day species
